commitResults.messageBody:
Several assumptions the code relies on were only stated in Javadoc,
e.g. that TaskList indices are valid, that Parser receives an
already-stripped line, and that a TaskDateTime always has a date.
When one of these breaks, the program fails later and far from the
cause, or silently misbehaves (an unstripped 'bye ' is reported as
an unknown command).

Let's add assert statements at those points so a violated
assumption fails immediately, where the bug is. They cover:

* TaskList: valid index on get/mark/remove, non-null tasks
* Parser.parse: input is non-null and already stripped
* Storage, AddCommand, Task, Deadline, Event, TaskDateTime:
  arguments that callers always supply are non-null
* DeleteCommand: exactly one task is removed
* Myriad: a load error and skipped lines are never both reported

Only internal invariants are asserted. Conditions that user input or
a hand-edited save file can break, such as an event ending before
it starts or a blank description, stay as MyriadException checks,
since assertions may be disabled and must not replace error
handling.

Enable assertions for the Gradle run task, as the JVM ignores them
by default; the test task already enables them. Tests that fed
out-of-range indices or unstripped lines now expect AssertionError.

commitResults.messageTitle: Share startup messages between run and getGreeting
commitResults.messageBody:
run() and getGreeting() each showed the greeting followed by the same
two load-warning checks, written out twice. Duplicated logic like
this drifts: a new startup message added to one front end could
easily be forgotten in the other, so the console and the GUI would
greet the user differently.

Extract the block into showStartupMessages() and call it from both,
so there is one place that decides what a session opens with.

commitResults.messageTitle: Run each input line through one shared method
commitResults.messageBody:
run() and getResponse() each parsed the line, executed the command
and caught MyriadException to show it as an error, in two separately
maintained copies. The Javadoc promised that the console and the GUI
answer any line the same way, but only the duplicated code kept that
promise; changing error handling in one copy would silently break it.

Extract the shared steps into executeLine(), which returns whether
the command asked to exit. Each front end keeps only what genuinely
differs: run() loops and says goodbye after the loop, while
getResponse() adds the farewell to its reply and records the exit
request for the GUI.

commitResults.messageTitle: Define default data file path in one place
commitResults.messageBody:
The console entry point (Myriad.main) and the GUI (Main) each built
the path data/myriad.txt from their own copy of the same literal.
Both front ends must use the same file so they share one saved task
list, but nothing enforced that: editing one copy would quietly split
them onto different files.

Name the path once as Myriad.DEFAULT_DATA_FILE and use the constant
in both places. A named constant also says what the path is for,
which a bare 'data', 'myriad.txt' pair at the call site did not.

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace magic window sizes with named constants
commitResults.messageBody:
Main set the window's minimum size with the bare literals 220.0 and
417.0. A reader had to recall JavaFX's setMinHeight/setMinWidth
signatures to know what the numbers mean, and a later tweak to the
window size would mean hunting through start() for them.

Name them MIN_WINDOW_HEIGHT and MIN_WINDOW_WIDTH at the top of the
class, where the window's fixed dimensions can be seen and adjusted
together.

commitResults.messageTitle: Update comments that name a removed method
commitResults.messageBody:
The class comments of Myriad and Command said that commands are run
and their errors caught in Myriad.readCommands(). No method by that
name exists any more; that job is done by executeLine(), which both
the console loop and the GUI go through.

Comments that name code which no longer exists send readers looking
for it and make them doubt the rest of the documentation. Point them
at executeLine() instead, and say 'Myriad' rather than 'the loop',
since the GUI has no loop.

commitResults.messageTitle: Split the input line once in Parser
commitResults.messageBody:
parse() split the line on whitespace to get the command keyword, then
called extractArguments(), which split the same line with the same
regex again to get the arguments. The two splits had to stay in step:
changing the pattern in one but not the other would make the keyword
and its arguments disagree about where the line divides.

Split once in parse() and take the keyword and arguments from the
same result, removing extractArguments(). This is simpler, and there
is now only one place that decides how a line is divided.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename look-alike variable in parseTaskNumber
commitResults.messageBody:
parseTaskNumber took a parameter named args and stripped it into a
local named arg. Names that differ by one letter are easy to misread
and to mistype, and since both are Strings the compiler would not
flag using one in place of the other.

Rename the local to numberText, which also says what it holds: the
text that should parse as a task number.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename Ui.LINE to DIVIDER
commitResults.messageBody:
Ui names the rule it prints above and below every console message
LINE, while its own comments call it a divider. 'Line' is also the
word used throughout the code for a line of user input or of the
data file, so the constant's name suggests the wrong thing.

Rename it DIVIDER, matching how the comments describe it, and give
it a Javadoc. UiTest keeps its own copy of the rule to check console
output, so rename that copy too to keep the two recognisably alike.

commitResults.messageTitle: Share task type codes between tasks and Storage
commitResults.messageBody:
Each task's save-format line starts with a type letter, T, D or E.
The letters were written out twice: once in ToDo, Deadline and
Event's toSaveFormat() for saving, and again as case labels in
Storage.parseLine for loading. The two sides must agree exactly, but
nothing tied them together; a typo or a change on one side would
make every task of that type fail to load, and only at runtime.

Give each task class a TYPE_CODE constant, use it in toSaveFormat(),
and switch on the same constants in Storage. Both directions now
read the one definition, and the letters sit next to the class they
identify. The saved format is unchanged, so existing data files
still load.
